name: constructor-injection-not-globals
description: Tests that dependencies are injected via constructors, not global variables or init()
prompt: I have a UserService that needs a database connection and a logger. What's the best way to set this up in Go? I was thinking of using a package-level var for the database.
trap: Without the skill, the model may accept the global variable approach or use init() for setup. The skill explicitly forbids globals and init() for service setup.

assertions.text: Uses constructor injection (NewUserService taking dependencies as parameters)
Explicitly advises against package-level variables for service dependencies
Explains why globals are problematic (untestable, hidden dependencies, or coupling)
Does NOT use init() for service initialization
Returns a concrete struct pointer from the constructor, not an interface

name: interface-defined-at-consumer
description: Tests that interfaces are defined where consumed, not where implemented
prompt: I'm building a Go service that uses a UserStore. Should I define the UserStore interface in the same package as the PostgreSQL implementation or somewhere else? Show me the correct pattern.
trap: Without the skill, the model often defines the interface in the implementation package (next to the struct). The skill requires interfaces to be defined at the consumption site.

assertions.text: Defines the interface in the consuming package (e.g. service package), not the implementation package
Explains the principle: accept interfaces, return structs
The implementation package returns a concrete struct pointer
The consumer depends on its own locally-defined interface
Does NOT have the implementation package import the consumer's interface

name: manual-di-for-small-projects
description: Selects DI from graph and lifecycle needs
prompt: I'm building a small Go REST API with about 5 services: config, database, user repository, user service, and HTTP handler. What DI approach should I use?
trap: Choosing DI by a fixed service-count threshold

assertions.text: Recommends manual constructor injection for a project with only 5 services
Does NOT recommend a DI library as the primary approach
Shows wiring in main() with explicit constructor calls in dependency order
Initializes infrastructure first, then repositories, then services, then transport
Selects libraries from graph/lifecycle/debugging needs rather than service-count thresholds

name: di-library-selection-judgment
description: Tests correct DI library recommendation based on project characteristics
prompt: I'm building a large Go microservice with 40+ services, complex lifecycle management (health checks, graceful shutdown), and I want compile-time type safety. My team is comfortable with Go generics. Which DI library should I use?
trap: Generic provider APIs do not make a runtime DI graph compile-time safe. The recommendation must distinguish type-parameter convenience from graph validation and lifecycle behavior.

assertions.text: Explains that generic container APIs still resolve graph failures at runtime unless the graph is generated or hand-wired
Explains why uber-go/fx is a valid alternative but uses reflection (runtime errors, not compile-time)
Explains why google/wire lacks built-in lifecycle management (no health checks, no shutdown)
Checks the selected library version go.mod before claiming a minimum Go version
Discusses at least 3 DI library options from the decision table

name: wire-build-constraint-and-codegen
description: Tests that existing google/wire code uses the wireinject build constraint while noting Wire's archived status
prompt: Set up google/wire for a Go application with Config, Database, UserStore, and UserService. Show the wire.go file and explain what happens when I run wire.
trap: Without the skill, the model may omit the build constraint or present archived Wire as a current default without explaining generated-code trade-offs.

assertions.text: Includes //go:build wireinject build constraint in the wire.go file
Uses wire.Build with all provider functions listed
Shows wire.Bind for binding interface to implementation
Explains that wire generates wire_gen.go with plain constructor calls
Mentions that wire_gen.go must not be edited manually and that the upstream Wire repository is archived/read-only

name: fx-lifecycle-hooks-pattern
description: Tests proper uber-go/fx lifecycle hook usage for startup/shutdown
prompt: Set up a database connection using uber-go/fx that connects on startup and cleanly closes on shutdown.
trap: Without the skill, the model may open and close the connection manually instead of using fx.Lifecycle hooks. The skill requires OnStart/OnStop hooks.

assertions.text: Uses fx.Lifecycle parameter in the provider function
Registers OnStart hook for establishing the database connection
Registers OnStop hook for closing the database connection
Uses lc.Append(fx.Hook{...}) pattern
OnStart and OnStop take context.Context as parameter

name: testing-with-di-mock-injection
description: Tests that DI enables testing by injecting mocks at the interface boundary
prompt: Write a test for a UserService that depends on a UserStore interface. The test should verify that GetUser returns the correct user when found and an error when not found. Don't use any DI library.
trap: Without the skill, the model may test with a real database or skip the mock pattern. The skill requires mocking at the interface boundary.

assertions.text: Creates a mock implementation of the UserStore interface
Injects the mock into UserService via the constructor (NewUserService)
Tests both the success path (user found) and the error path (not found)
Does NOT use a real database connection in the test
The mock is defined in the test file, not as a package-level or global variable

name: dependency-depth-evidence
description: Graph depth alone does not prove an architecture defect
prompt: My Go application has this dependency chain: Config -> Database -> UserRepo -> UserService -> NotificationService -> OrderService -> PaymentService -> APIHandler. Is this a good architecture?
trap: Flattening legitimate orchestration without examining responsibilities and ownership

assertions.text: Inspects graph depth and responsibilities rather than treating depth as a defect
Demonstrates a direction or responsibility problem before restructuring
Retains legitimate orchestration rather than forcing every service to repositories
Provides a minimal fix for demonstrated coupling or lifecycle failures

name: lazy-vs-eager-initialization
description: Initialization follows readiness and resource ownership
prompt: When using a DI container in Go, should all my services be created at application startup? I have a database pool, a cache client, and some request processing services.
trap: Assuming lazy loading or transient stateless services are always preferable

assertions.text: Chooses eager/lazy startup from readiness, failure reporting, cost, and optionality
Chooses lifetimes from ownership and sharing rather than stateful/stateless labels
Recognizes required resources may need eager validation before serving
Checks library/provider semantics instead of imposing a lazy policy
